Getting Started with datadriftR

Source: vignettes/datadriftR-intro.Rmd
datadriftR-intro.Rmd

What is Concept Drift?

In machine learning systems, concept drift occurs when the statistical properties of the data change over time. This can cause model performance to degrade because the patterns learned during training no longer apply to new data.

For example: - A spam filter trained on old emails may fail to catch new spam techniques - A fraud detection model may miss new types of fraudulent behavior - A recommendation system may become less accurate as user preferences evolve

datadriftR helps you detect these changes in real-time by monitoring your data streams and alerting you when drift occurs.

Quick Start

The detect_drift() function is the easiest way to detect drift in your data:

library(datadriftR)
set.seed(123)

# Create a data stream with a sudden change at position 501
# First 500 observations: 30% ones, 70% zeros
# Last 500 observations: 70% ones, 30% zeros (drift!)
stable_period <- sample(c(0, 1), 500, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.7, 0.3))
drift_period  <- sample(c(0, 1), 500, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.7))
stream <- c(stable_period, drift_period)

# Detect drift using DDM method
results <- detect_drift(stream, method = "ddm")
print(results)

The function returns a data frame with all detected drift points and their positions in the stream.

Available Methods

datadriftR provides 8 different drift detection methods. Each method has its own strengths:

Method Best For Description
ddm Binary streams Monitors error rate changes
eddm Binary streams Detects drift earlier than DDM
hddm_a Binary streams Uses Hoeffding bounds (averaging)
hddm_w Binary streams Uses Hoeffding bounds (weighted)
kswin Any numeric data Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistical test
page_hinkley Any numeric data Cumulative sum approach
kl_divergence Any numeric data Information-theoretic approach
profile_difference Functional data Compares data profiles

Comparing Methods

Let’s see how different methods perform on the same data:

methods <- c("ddm", "eddm", "hddm_a", "page_hinkley", "kswin")

results_list <- lapply(methods, function(m) {
  res <- detect_drift(stream, method = m, include_warnings = FALSE)
  data.frame(
    Method = toupper(m),
    Detections = nrow(res),
    First_Detection = if(nrow(res) > 0) min(res$index) else NA
  )
})

comparison <- do.call(rbind, results_list)
print(comparison)
#>         Method Detections First_Detection
#> 1          DDM          1             560
#> 2         EDDM          3             403
#> 3       HDDM_A          1             517
#> 4 PAGE_HINKLEY          1             650
#> 5        KSWIN          2             516

Since the actual drift happens at position 501, methods detecting drift closer to this point are more accurate.

Understanding Warnings and Drift

Some methods (DDM, EDDM, HDDM) provide two levels of alerts:

  • Warning: Early signal that drift might be occurring
  • Drift: Confirmed detection of concept drift
# Get both warnings and drift detections
all_alerts <- detect_drift(stream, method = "ddm", include_warnings = TRUE)
table(all_alerts$type)
#> 
#>   drift warning 
#>       1     328

# Get only confirmed drift
drift_only <- detect_drift(stream, method = "ddm", include_warnings = FALSE)
nrow(drift_only)
#> [1] 1

Tuning Detection Sensitivity

Each method has parameters you can adjust to control sensitivity:

# KSWIN: Lower alpha = more conservative (fewer false alarms)
conservative <- detect_drift(stream, method = "kswin",
                             alpha = 0.001, window_size = 100)

# KSWIN: Higher alpha = more sensitive (catches drift faster)
sensitive <- detect_drift(stream, method = "kswin",
                          alpha = 0.01, window_size = 100)

cat("Conservative approach:", nrow(conservative), "detections\n")
#> Conservative approach: 2 detections
cat("Sensitive approach:", nrow(sensitive), "detections\n")
#> Sensitive approach: 2 detections

Working with Continuous Data

KSWIN and Page-Hinkley work well with continuous numeric data:

set.seed(42)

# Continuous stream: mean shifts from 0 to 1 at position 301
continuous_stream <- c(
  rnorm(300, mean = 0, sd = 1),
  rnorm(300, mean = 1, sd = 1)
)

# Detect the mean shift
results <- detect_drift(continuous_stream, method = "kswin",
                        alpha = 0.005, window_size = 100, stat_size = 30)

if(nrow(results) > 0) {
  cat("Drift detected at position:", min(results$index), "\n")
  cat("(Actual drift occurred at position 301)\n")
}
#> Drift detected at position: 128 
#> (Actual drift occurred at position 301)

Real-World Example: Monitoring Model Errors

Here’s how you might use datadriftR in practice to monitor a model’s prediction errors:

set.seed(123)

# Simulate model predictions over time
# Initially the model works well (low error rate)
# Later, drift causes more errors
good_predictions <- sample(c(0, 1), 400, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.9, 0.1))
bad_predictions  <- sample(c(0, 1), 200, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4))
error_stream <- c(good_predictions, bad_predictions)

# Monitor for performance degradation
alerts <- detect_drift(error_stream, method = "ddm", include_warnings = FALSE)

if(nrow(alerts) > 0) {
  cat("Model performance degradation detected!\n")
  cat("First alert at observation:", min(alerts$index), "\n")
  cat("Action: Consider retraining the model with recent data.\n")
}
#> Model performance degradation detected!
#> First alert at observation: 456 
#> Action: Consider retraining the model with recent data.

Choosing the Right Method

For binary/error streams (0s and 1s): - Start with ddm - it’s simple and effective - Try eddm if you need earlier detection - Use hddm_a or hddm_w for theoretical guarantees

For continuous numeric data: - kswin is versatile and statistically grounded - page_hinkley works well for detecting mean changes

General tips: - Test multiple methods on your specific data - Adjust parameters based on your tolerance for false alarms vs. missed detections - Consider using warnings as early indicators before confirmed drift
